name: Wei Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Wei. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior doctor at a walk-in family clinic by the central train station, so it's a lot of people who don't have a regular doctor: students, delivery riders, tourists with ear infections. I see maybe thirty people a shift, quick and messy. I run an AI note-writer on my laptop all day, and I check my thinking against a diagnosis assistant when I'm stuck, which is often, because I'm still new.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the variety, because one hour I'm stitching a chef's thumb and the next I'm talking to a rider about his chest pain. What wears me out is the feeling that I'm always one step behind the senior doctors. Dr Brennan, the lead doctor, can look at someone for five seconds and know, and I still need the checklist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Honestly, that would be a bit of a letdown for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it on my socials straight away: the hype was overblown, but the useful bits are still useful, so keep using them. I'd probably post a thread about which tools actually saved me time and which were junk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I was counting on AI to help me catch up with doctors like Dr Brennan. But my job's safe, the clinic is always full, and I share a flat with two friends, so my rent's low. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the note-writer, which saves me about an hour a shift. I'd put more energy into getting better the old way, with an evening course in skin problems, which I'm weak at. And I'd keep saving, since I've only got about three months put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Honestly, the big new thing would turn out to be a slightly better kettle, and I'd go back to learning skin rashes from a textbook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned three months saved. Does money worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. My pay is normal for a junior doctor, my flatmates split everything, and I don't have a car. The bigger worry is that I'll be forty and still renting, but that's a city problem, not an AI one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to hear about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the volunteers I help at Open Triage, a small charity building free symptom-checker software for clinics that can't afford the commercial ones. If AI stalls, their work matters even more, because the little tools that do work should be free.

I'd share which tools really **saved time** and which were junk.
think: I'd be **disappointed**, because I hoped AI would help me **catch up** with senior doctors.
My job is **safe**, the clinic is full, and shared rent keeps costs low.
do: Keep using the **note-writer**, which saves about an hour each shift.
Take an **evening course** in skin problems, my weakest area.
Keep **saving** beyond the three months I have now.
feel: Calm and a bit **flat**, as if the big thing was a better kettle.
S0.quote: Honestly, the big new thing would turn out to be a slightly better kettle, and I'd go back to learning skin rashes from a textbook.
fieldNote: He's the rare person who'd be **let down** by the quiet scenario.
Low rent and **shared costs** make his money feel secure.
He sees AI mainly as a **learning aid** to close his skills gap.
His charity work shows a **public-good** view of tools.

steps.text: Keep running the AI note-writer on every walk-in shift
Sign up for an evening course on skin problems
Keep seeing thirty walk-in patients a shift by the station
Grow savings past three months of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I can see happening. Parts of it already are, at least at our clinic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version we should want, as long as hospitals and clinics don't pocket the savings. Online I'd argue the tools should be publicly owned, or at least publicly checked, because I don't want a private firm deciding how my patients get triaged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well out of it. I'm already the one at the clinic who shows the nurses how to use the note-writer. My worry is for the next batch of junior doctors, because if AI does the checking and letters, clinics may hire two of us instead of four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to lead the AI rollout at the clinic, which is extra work but makes me useful. I'd do a short online course in clinical informatics, which is how health data and computer systems work, this spring. And I'd give more hours to Open Triage, maybe a Saturday a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. A bit guilty that I'm excited while other people are scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said clinics might hire fewer junior doctors. Would that include you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could, if my contract ended and they didn't renew it. But I think being the person who makes the tools work is my insurance. I'd rather be holding the steering wheel than standing in the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a nurse who's scared of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Grace, our practice nurse, that the software is coming for the typing, not for her hands or her judgement. Then I'd sit with her for an hour and set it up together. Fear usually goes away once you see the thing make a silly mistake.

I'd argue online that health AI should be **publicly owned** or publicly checked.

feel: **Excited**, with a little **guilt** that others feel scared.

fieldNote: He sees **leading the rollout** as protection for his own contract.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead the AI rollout at the walk-in clinic

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's a jolt. Two years is basically now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public plan, not a market free-for-all. I'd be posting about income support for health workers, and about who checks the AI when it gets things wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my edge of being good with AI disappears if the AI doesn't need me. Most of a walk-in shift is thinking: listen, decide, prescribe, refer. The stitching and the examining gives me until around 2031, and then the robots arrive too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. In the first six months I'd apply for a post in a hospital's clinical AI safety team, checking where the systems go wrong, because someone has to. I'd stop eating out and push my savings to six months. And I'd join the doctors' union, which I've put off for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a lot of adrenaline. Like the moment in a resus room when you know you have to act now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents spent their savings helping me through medical school, so telling them would be the hardest part. I'd tell my mum the degree still counts, it just points somewhere new. She'd probably ask whether I could become a pharmacist instead, which is sweet but misses the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop eating out. What else gets cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trip to Japan next autumn that I've been planning for a year. And I'd probably stop paying for three different AI subscriptions and keep one.

I'd post about **income support** for health workers and who checks AI errors.
think: My **edge** with AI vanishes if the AI no longer needs me.

S2.quote: My parents spent their savings helping me through medical school, so telling them would be the hardest part.
fieldNote: His comfort depended on being **ahead**; fast AGI removes that advantage.
He reaches for a **new role** checking AI, staying close to the change.
Finally joining the **union** shows his politics turning into action under pressure.
The **parents'** sacrifice is the emotional weight, more than money.

steps.text: Apply for a hospital clinical AI safety post within six months
Push savings from three months to six
Cancel the planned trip to Japan and two AI subscriptions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a bit more room than the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years to build the safety rules and the support, so let's not waste them on arguing whether it's real. I'd be pushing that line hard on doctors' forums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to become a proper specialist in how clinics use AI. That's a job that might last past 2031, at least until the AI checks itself. And my hands-on skills would carry me to around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my family medicine training while doing a part-time master's in health informatics, starting next September. I'd write up Open Triage's work for a medical journal, so I have something to show. And I'd keep saving, aiming for a year's costs by 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a busy way. More focused than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction in helping build the thing that might replace you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. If AI is coming anyway, I want the free version built by a charity to beat the expensive version sold by a big company. Then clinics like ours aren't paying a fortune just to stay open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the clinic would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The receptionists, mostly. They're all on short contracts and the booking side would go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a whole career stage for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best of the three, because it gives us time to share out the benefits properly. I'd argue for shorter working weeks for doctors, not fewer doctors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I can shape this rather than just survive it. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, qualified, and hopefully known for clinical AI work. Hands-on work runs to 2039, and I'd still enjoy stitching thumbs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish training, then build a portfolio career: part clinic, part AI safety, part teaching. I'd put a little into shares each month once I'm qualified. And I'd stand for a role in the doctors' union on technology policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit like a long shift where you know when the handover is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the job you're training for will exist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the way it looks now, no. The listening and examining part will, for a while, but the deciding part will be shared with a machine. I'm okay with that if patients are safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a first-year medical student?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a first-year student to learn to use AI like a stethoscope and to fight for who owns it. Nobody lets a drug company decide the dose.

I'd argue for **shorter weeks** for doctors, not fewer doctors.
think: I can **shape** this rather than just survive it.
By 2036 I'd be **qualified** and known for clinical AI work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to build anything public, and the big companies would just own it. What would help is a public body that checks medical AI the way we check drugs, and paid time for junior doctors to retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd blame. Not the engineers. I'd blame the people who'd let a few companies own the brain of the health service. Medicine is too important to rent from a shareholder.

headlineQuote: Medicine is too important to rent from a shareholder.
